sections.section_title: Initial Presentation, Exposure History, and Early Sepsis Management
sections.description: This section outlines the patient’s presenting symptoms, vital signs, and key laboratory abnormalities that prompted a diagnosis of severe sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) following a dog bite. It emphasizes the importance of a thorough exposure history and rapid stabilization measures.
subtopics: Timeline of events from dog bite to hospital admission
Physical findings: fever, mottled extremities, hypoglycaemia, and neurologic status
Initial laboratory panel: pancytopenia, coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, lactate, renal and hepatic dysfunction
Rapid assessment tools: qSOFA, DIC scoring systems
Empiric antimicrobial coverage for animal‑related pathogens (piperacillin‑tazobactam, later ampicillin)
Supportive care: fluid resuscitation, glucose management, blood product transfusion, ICU admission

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis and Diagnostic Work‑up During the Septic Phase
sections.description: Focuses on the breadth of potential diagnoses entertained when a patient with sepsis develops multi‑organ failure, pancytopenia, and coagulopathy, and details the investigations performed to rule out competing entities before the TMA became evident.
subtopics: Broad differential for pancytopenia and DIC: acute leukemia, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, severe bacterial sepsis, toxin‑mediated syndromes
Targeted hematologic work‑up: peripheral smear, flow cytometry, bone‑marrow considerations
Infectious work‑up: blood cultures (identification of Capnocytophaga canimorsus), molecular methods, imaging to exclude necrotising fasciitis
Autoimmune screening (ANA, ANCA) and exclusion of vasculitis
Renal assessment: urinalysis, ultrasound, need for renal replacement therapy
Interpretation of early thrombotic phenomena as DIC versus evolving microangiopathy

sections.section_title: Transition to Thrombotic Microangiopathy: Diagnostic Reasoning and Confirmation
sections.description: Describes the clinical clues that signaled a shift from sepsis‑related DIC to a true thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), the step‑wise laboratory evaluation to classify the TMA, and the definitive tissue diagnosis via kidney biopsy.
subtopics: New onset hemolysis: falling hemoglobin, undetectable haptoglobin, rising LDH, schistocytes on smear
Persistent thrombocytopenia despite resolution of DIC parameters
Evaluation for TTP: PLASMIC score, ADAMTS13 activity (43.5 %), role of plasma exchange as bridge therapy
Exclusion of STEC‑HUS: stool PCR for Shiga toxin, absence of diarrheal prodrome
Complement testing: C3/C4, functional pathway assays, alternative pathway activity (AH50) after plasma exchange and eculizumab
Kidney biopsy findings: acute tubular necrosis, fibrin thrombi, ischemic glomeruli, crescents – histologic confirmation of TMA
Final diagnostic synthesis leading to complement‑mediated HUS (CM‑HUS) diagnosis

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of Complement‑Mediated HUS and the Role of Capnocytophaga canimorsus
sections.description: Provides a concise yet comprehensive review of alternative‑pathway complement dysregulation underlying CM‑HUS, the concept of a ‘second hit’ by infection, and how C. canimorsus can act as a trigger in genetically susceptible or immunocompetent hosts.
subtopics: Alternative complement pathway activation and regulatory proteins (factor H, I, B, CD46)
Genetic predisposition versus acquired triggers; prevalence of complement‑gene variants in atypical HUS
Mechanisms by which C. canimorsus interacts with complement: capsule resistance, serum susceptibility, endotoxin‑like activation
Why complement activation can paradoxically cause endothelial injury and TMA
Review of reported cases linking C. canimorsus to CM‑HUS and comparative genetics
Implications of normal C3/C4 levels during active disease

sections.section_title: Therapeutic Strategy, Clinical Outcomes, and Lessons Learned
sections.description: Summarizes the therapeutic interventions—plasma exchange, eculizumab, vaccination, and antimicrobial prophylaxis—highlighting timing considerations, challenges of treating complement blockade during infection, and the patient’s renal and hematologic recovery trajectory.
subtopics: Rationale for plasma exchange as interim therapy in suspected TMA
Eculizumab initiation: dosing schedule, pre‑treatment meningococcal vaccination, antibiotic prophylaxis
Balancing infection control with complement inhibition; safety precautions for encapsulated organisms
Renal replacement therapy weaning and partial recovery of kidney function
Long‑term management: maintenance eculizumab, monitoring for relapse, genetic testing follow‑up
Prognostic factors in CM‑HUS (time to complement blockade, baseline renal function)
Key teaching points: early recognition of infection‑triggered TMA, systematic exclusion of TTP/STEC‑HUS, importance of interdisciplinary coordination
